title: Rethinking Calibration for Early-Exit Neural Networks
claim: Calibration-based confidence forces futile samples through every stage, while our correction lets the model exit early and save compute.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right layers, pink and yellow highlight regions with skipped dashed boxes
description: A wide diagram shows a ligertiger photo at top left feeding a chain of blue feature boxes (Features 1, 2, 3, ...) linked by Block arrows. Each feature box drops via a Head arrow to an orange prediction box, such as Pred.: Lion, Conf 0.38, marked with a red X. Beneath, a yellow-shaded band shows the calibration path: Calib. arrows lead to boxes with Conf below tau reading CONT., with the label 'Calibration results in wasted compute.' A pink-shaded path labeled EEFP CC runs from the first head straight down to a red-bordered box, Conf 0.88 at or above tau, EXIT. Later EEFP CC arrows are greyed and dashed, leading to grey 'Skipped' boxes. The eye goes first to the photo, then to the contrast between yellow and pink regions.
caption: Conceptual comparison between standard confidence calibration and our proposed method for early-exit failure prediction. We consider a "futile" sample, which no exit in the model can classify correctly. Standard Calibration (yellow): Calibration equates reliability with the probability of correctness, resulting in low confidence (less than exit confidence threshold $\tau$) for samples the model is likely to get wrong. This forces the sample to traverse the entire architecture, causing significant computational waste. EEFP Confidence Correction (purple): Our method detects cases for which additional effort is futile, enabling the model to assign high exit confidence and halt execution immediately.
abstract: Early-exit neural networks (EENNs) accelerate inference by allowing intermediate classifiers to stop computation once predictions are confident enough. Most methods rely on confidence thresholds for exiting, and consequently, improving classifier calibration is widely assumed to improve performance. In this work, we challenge this assumption and show that calibration alone is not sufficient for EENNs to exploit adaptive computation. To address this insufficiency, we introduce Early-Exit Failure Prediction (EEFP), which accounts for both prediction correctness and the cost of further computation. We also propose a lightweight, EEFP-motivated procedure to improve the intermediate classifiers, which can directly replace calibration in EENNs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves superior cost-accuracy trade-offs compared to calibration, and EEFP more reliably reflects overall EENN performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/gmum/rethinking-calibration-for-eenns.
